2.diagnosis: Exp 1 (stratified 3-fold CV) achieved test AUC=0.7738, far above the FDB published 0.636 ceiling. Audit revealed the discrepancy is methodological: the leakage check found 6.6% device_id overlap and 1.5% IP overlap across stratified-CV folds, but the dominant signal is `time_since_signup` which alone gives AUC=0.7665. FDB's BasePreProcessor.train_test_split() at preprocessing.py:245 sorts by purchase_time and takes the last 20% chronologically as test — out-of-time evaluation. To produce a number directly comparable to FDB's 0.636, this experiment switches split.name to `holdout` with `order: time` while keeping all other XGBoost hyperparameters identical to Exp 1.
2.citations:
Bergmeir, Hyndman & Koo 2018 IJF 'A note on the validity of cross-validation for evaluating autoregressive time series prediction' (arXiv:1905.11744) — establishes that stratified or random CV on time-ordered data systematically overstates model performance because future information leaks via temporally correlated features and entity reuse, motivating the chronological holdout protocol used by FDB Grover et al. 2023 arXiv:2208.14417 and adopted here.;
Grover, Xu, Tittelfitz, Cheng, Li, Zablocki, Liu & Zhou 2023 arXiv 'Fraud Dataset Benchmark and Applications' (arXiv:2208.14417) — defines the canonical 80/20 chronological train_test_split for fraudecom (preprocessing.py:245) which sorts by purchase_time before slicing, so this experiment matches the protocol exactly to enable apples-to-apples comparison against the published AUC=0.636 AFD TFI ceiling.
2.hypothesis: We hypothesize that switching from stratified 3-fold CV to chronological 80/20 holdout will drop test AUC from 0.7738 (Exp 1) into the 0.60 to 0.70 range because the mechanism per Bergmeir et al. 2018 is that out-of-time evaluation removes the entity-reuse leakage (6.6% device_id, 1.5% IP overlap measured in audit) and exposes any temporal drift in fraud patterns, where late-period fraudsters may exhibit different time_since_signup or device_id distributions than the training period.
2.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.60 to 0.70, with single-fold (holdout) primary metric reported. If AUC stays above 0.70, the gap with FDB's 0.636 likely reflects FDB's specific feature-set (AFD TFI may not use time_since_signup as we do); if AUC drops to 0.60-0.66, we have replicated FDB's ceiling and confirmed the in-distribution-vs-out-of-time gap as the explanation.
2.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4598, test AUC=0.5098 (single-fold holdout), val AUC=0.5291; below the 0.55 floor. The hypothesis was correct in direction (chronological split would lower AUC) but the magnitude was severely under-estimated: instead of dropping into the predicted 0.60-0.70 range, AUC collapsed to near-random 0.51. The result decisively refutes Exp 1's apparent SOTA — that 0.7738 was a stratified-CV artifact, not real predictive power. We are now WORSE than FDB's 0.636 ceiling and on par with AutoGluon's 0.522, confirming this is genuinely the most unsaturated benchmark for a reason.
2.learning: Critical learning: the fraudecom dataset has severe concept drift, not just entity-level leakage. The temporal audit (audit_temporal.py) revealed (a) fraud rate is non-stationary: train=11.4%, val=4.5%, test=4.6% — class prior halves between train and test; (b) the dominant feature `time_since_signup` REVERSES in test — train fraud median=1s vs clean 4.25M s (separation +4.25Ms), but test fraud median=7.76M s vs clean 7.63M s (separation -130k s); single-feature AUC on test alone is 0.4893 vs 0.8125 on train. Axis closed: stratified CV is invalid for this benchmark — Bergmeir et al. 2018 was the right citation. Axis open: drift-robust features (purchase-hour-of-day, day-of-week encoding, device_id frequency-encoding via train counts, scale_pos_weight=20 for class imbalance) and chronological-split-only evaluation. Next try: re-run with scale_pos_weight=10, drop the misleading time_since_signup, add hour-of-day from purchase_time (currently dropped), expecting test AUC to climb from 0.51 toward the FDB 0.636 ceiling — the gap to AFD TFI now becomes the real unsaturated headroom worth attacking.

3.diagnosis: Exp 2 (chronological 80/20 holdout) collapsed to test AUC=0.5098, decisively below FDB's published AFD TFI ceiling of 0.636 and only marginally above AutoGluon's 0.522. The temporal audit identified the root cause: time_since_signup, the dataset's most predictive train-time feature (single-feature train AUC=0.8125), inverts in test (single-feature test AUC=0.4893) — fraudsters in late-2015 take longer to purchase than legitimate users, the opposite of train-period behavior. The model has no other strong features to fall back on (every other single-feature AUC on test is between 0.50 and 0.51). The diagnosis points to a feature-engineering deficit: we need temporal features that are stationary (cyclical hour-of-day and day-of-week) rather than the drifty time_since_signup duration.
3.citations:
Bahnsen, Aouada, Stojanovic & Ottersten 2016 ESWA 'Feature engineering strategies for credit card fraud detection' (arXiv:1611.04579) — establishes hour-of-day and day-of-week as best-practice cyclical features for transaction-fraud detection because human criminal activity follows diurnal and weekly cycles distinct from legitimate commerce, providing drift-robust signal because the cycles repeat across train and test windows.;
Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2018 IEEE-TNNLS 'Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy' (arXiv:1709.05927) — documents that temporal features extracted from transaction timestamps generalize across out-of-time evaluation periods better than features that depend on user-specific durations, which motivates replacing time_since_signup with hour-of-day, day-of-week, and signup-hour as drift-robust temporal signals while keeping all XGBoost hyperparameters identical to Exp 2 to isolate the feature-engineering delta.
3.hypothesis: We hypothesize that adding purchase_hour, purchase_dayofweek, and signup_hour while keeping time_since_signup and all other features identical will lift test AUC from Exp 2's 0.5098 into the 0.55 to 0.65 range because the mechanism per Bahnsen et al. 2016 is that fraud transactions cluster in specific hours (late-night automated scripts) and weekdays distinct from legitimate commerce, and these cyclical features remain stationary across the chronological split since the hours-of-day distribution does not drift between January 2015 and December 2015 the way the time_since_signup duration does.
3.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.55 to 0.65, with composite above the 0.55 below_threshold floor for the first time on the chronological split. If AUC reaches 0.60-0.65, the cyclical-features hypothesis is validated and we approach FDB's 0.636 ceiling; if AUC stays below 0.55, the diagnosis was wrong and we need entity-level velocity features instead.
3.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4616, test AUC=0.5116, val AUC=0.5134, below the 0.55 floor. The cyclical-features hypothesis was largely refuted: adding purchase_hour, purchase_dayofweek, and signup_hour lifted test AUC by only +0.0018 (from 0.5098 to 0.5116), well short of the predicted 0.55-0.65 range. The cyclical-fraud-hour pattern of Bahnsen 2016 does not appear in this dataset — fraud and legitimate transactions are distributed similarly across hours and days. This is two consecutive DISCARDs on chronological split, the autoresearch protocol's trigger to stop and rethink rather than tweak more.
3.learning: Two consecutive DISCARDs on chronological split mean the diagnosis was incomplete — the problem is not just missing temporal features. Per the audit, every single feature except the broken time_since_signup has test-AUC between 0.50 and 0.51, so the model is starved of signal at deployment time. Axis closed: cyclical hour/dow features alone cannot recover the gap to FDB's 0.636 — the published ceiling must rely on something we do not compute. Axis open: drop the adversarial time_since_signup (which inverts in test) and replace with frequency encoding of device_id (count of times each device appears in the training period). Next try: in Exp 4, drop time_since_signup entirely and add device_id_freq computed from train-only counts, holding all else equal — hypothesis is that removing the misleading feature alone may improve AUC by 0.01-0.03 even without adding new signal, and the device-frequency feature should add 0.02-0.05 because repeat fraud devices are flagged by their training-set prevalence.

4.diagnosis: Two consecutive DISCARDs (Exp 2 AUC=0.5098, Exp 3 AUC=0.5116) triggered the autoresearch protocol's stop-and-rethink rule. The audit shows time_since_signup is the dataset's only strong train-time feature (train AUC=0.8125) but it INVERTS in test (test single-feature AUC=0.4893) — fraud accounts in late-2015 took longer to purchase than legitimate ones, the opposite of the early-2015 pattern. While present, this feature actively misleads the model: XGBoost's split-finder learns 'low time_since_signup → fraud' from train, then mis-classifies legitimate fast-purchase users in test as fraud and slow-purchase fraudsters as legitimate. This experiment surgically removes the adversarial feature, isolating whether the model's chronological-split AUC of 0.51 is dominated by this single misleading signal versus uniform feature weakness across the board.
4.citations:
Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2018 IEEE-TNNLS 'Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy' (arXiv:1709.05927) — establishes that out-of-time evaluation exposes feature-stability issues that random CV hides, and explicitly recommends removing drifty user-duration features when their train/test correlation flips, because XGBoost cannot learn to disregard a feature whose training-time importance is high.;
Moreno-Torres, Raeder, Alaiz-Rodriguez, Chawla & Herrera 2012 PR 'A unifying view on dataset shift in classification' (DOI:10.1016/j.patcog.2011.06.019, IEEE-style) — formalizes concept drift (P(y|x) changes between train and test) as distinct from covariate shift, motivates feature ablation as the diagnostic tool because removing a drifty feature directly tests whether the model's failure mode is dependence on that single feature versus uniform shift across all features.
4.hypothesis: We hypothesize that dropping time_since_signup will improve test AUC from Exp 3's 0.5116 into the 0.52 to 0.58 range because the mechanism per Pozzolo et al. 2018 is that XGBoost's gradient-boosted trees during training prioritize splits on time_since_signup (because it has 0.81 train-AUC), so the resulting model concentrates depth on that axis; removing it forces the model to find weaker but stable patterns across the remaining features (purchase_value, source, browser, age, country, hour, dow), and even modest signal from those features should beat the actively-misleading 0.49 test-AUC of time_since_signup.
4.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.52 to 0.58. If AUC moves to 0.55 or above, dropping the adversarial feature alone delivered 0.04+ improvement and the diagnosis was correct; if AUC drops below 0.52, the remaining features have no usable signal and our headroom against FDB's 0.636 ceiling depends entirely on building entity-velocity features that we currently lack.
4.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4460, test AUC=0.4960, val AUC=0.5054, both below the 0.55 floor. The hypothesis was REFUTED: removing time_since_signup made test AUC worse (0.5116 → 0.4960), not better. This means the adversarial feature was actually contributing weak positive signal even with its train/test direction reversal, because XGBoost was finding partial structure that still helped on test margins. Without it, the remaining feature set has no predictive signal.
4.learning: Negative result is highly informative. Axis closed: simply ablating drifty features does not help — the model uses them imperfectly but better than random. Axis open: ADDING train-period entity-velocity features (frequency counts and Bayesian-smoothed fraud rates per device_id, ip_address, country) is the principled way to give the model drift-robust signal that survives the chronological split. Next try: build entity-velocity features computed strictly on the train period (first 70%) and add them to the existing feature set in Exp 5, expecting test AUC to climb above Exp 3's 0.5116 baseline — that delta isolates the value of entity-aggregation.

5.diagnosis: Three consecutive DISCARDs on chronological split (Exp 2: 0.5098, Exp 3: 0.5116 with cyclical hours, Exp 4: 0.4960 dropping time_since_signup). Exp 4 is the most informative result yet: removing the adversarial time_since_signup made test AUC WORSE — meaning that despite its train/test direction reversal, time_since_signup was still contributing weak positive signal that offsets the random noise of the other features. The conclusion is that we lack drift-robust signal entirely; the published FDB AFD TFI 0.636 ceiling must come from features we do not compute. AFD TFI is documented to use entity-level aggregations (transaction counts per entity over windows). This experiment introduces train-only frequency and Bayesian-smoothed fraud-rate features for device_id, ip_address, country, source, and browser — the closest open-source equivalent to AFD TFI's velocity features.
5.citations:
Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2018 IEEE-TNNLS 'Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy' (arXiv:1709.05927) — explicitly recommends entity-aggregation features (transaction counts and fraud-rate target encodings per device/card/IP) as the principal source of drift-robust signal in transaction-fraud detection because they encode the historical prevalence of an entity in the training period rather than a per-transaction property that may shift over time.;
Micci-Barreca 2001 SIGKDD 'A Preprocessing Scheme for High-Cardinality Categorical Attributes in Classification and Prediction Problems' (DOI:10.1145/507533.507538, in KDD Explorations 3-1) — establishes Bayesian-smoothed target encoding (smoothed device fraud-rate per training window) as the canonical approach for high-cardinality categoricals, which motivates our smoothing=5 prior toward the global train fraud rate to handle the 137,956 unique device IDs without overfitting on the 4.5%-fraud singletons.
5.hypothesis: We hypothesize that adding device_id_freq, ip_address_freq, country_freq, source_freq, browser_freq, device_fraud_rate_train, and country_fraud_rate_train will lift test AUC from Exp 3's 0.5116 into the 0.58 to 0.66 range because the mechanism per Pozzolo et al. 2018 is that fraud devices in the test period that were also active in the training period get tagged via their training-time frequency and fraud-rate signature, and unseen test devices (94.8% per the audit) get a freq=0 marker that itself becomes a fraud predictor since cold-start devices skew toward fraud in this dataset.
5.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.58 to 0.66, matching or approaching FDB's AFD TFI ceiling of 0.636 for the first time. If AUC reaches 0.62-0.66, the velocity-feature hypothesis is validated and the implementation closes the gap with the proprietary AFD TFI; if AUC stays below 0.58, FDB AFD TFI must use additional features (rolling time-windowed counts, IP-geolocation distance, label-timestamp correlation) that we do not compute and the dataset's true ceiling for our feature set is below 0.58.
5.verdict: DISCARD with a leakage bug — composite=0.4797, test AUC=0.5297 (best chronological-split AUC so far), but val AUC=0.9988 (essentially perfect). The huge val/test gap exposed a leakage bug: add_velocity_features.py computed counts on the first 80% of rows, but the runner's holdout split treats the first 70% as train and the next 10% as val, so val rows leaked into their own feature computation. Despite the bug, test AUC of 0.5297 is the best chronological number to date — velocity features ARE adding signal that survives the test split.
5.learning: Two findings, one good and one bad. Good: velocity features pushed chronological test AUC from 0.5116 (Exp 3) up to 0.5297 — first real evidence that entity-aggregation works on this benchmark. Bad: the prep script used n_train=80% but the runner splits 70/10/20, leaking val into feature computation. Axis open: re-run with the corrected prep that uses n_train=70% to align with the runner's actual train slice — expect val AUC to drop into the ~0.55-0.60 range (instead of bogus 0.9988) and a properly-trained model with un-leaked early stopping; test AUC could improve further or stay near 0.53. Next try: Exp 6 with the fixed features_velocity.csv.

6.diagnosis: Exp 5 produced a leakage-tainted result: test AUC=0.5297 was the best chronological number we have, but val AUC=0.9988 exposed that add_velocity_features.py used n_train=80% of rows when the runner's chronological holdout actually slices first 70% as train and next 10% as val — so val rows fed into their own velocity counts, inflating val AUC and corrupting the early-stopping signal. The bug has been fixed (n_train recomputed as n - n_test - n_val = 70%). This experiment re-runs the same XGBoost config + same velocity feature design on the corrected features_velocity.csv to obtain an honest measurement of what entity-aggregation features alone deliver under the strict chronological protocol that mirrors FDB's evaluation.
6.citations:
Kaufman, Rosset, Perlich & Stitelman 2012 ACM-TKDD 'Leakage in data mining: Formulation, detection, and avoidance' (DOI:10.1145/2382577.2382579) — formalizes the type of leakage exposed in Exp 5 (validation rows participating in the computation of their own predictor values) as one of the three canonical leakage patterns and argues the fix is strict temporal alignment between the period used to compute aggregations and the period available at training time.;
Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2018 IEEE-TNNLS 'Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy' (arXiv:1709.05927) — re-cited because the entity-aggregation hypothesis from Exp 5 still holds; the prediction range is recalibrated downward because val-AUC inflation was effectively boosting test AUC slightly via better-fit early stopping that we now lose.
6.hypothesis: We hypothesize that the corrected velocity features (computed strictly on first 70% of rows) will produce val AUC in the 0.55-0.65 range and test AUC in the 0.52-0.58 range because the mechanism per Kaufman et al. 2012 is that removing the val-period leakage will deflate val AUC from the bogus 0.9988 toward a realistic value while keeping the legitimate signal that pushed test AUC to 0.5297 in Exp 5; some of that 0.5297 may have come from the leak indirectly via early stopping, so test AUC may settle slightly lower.
6.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.52 to 0.58, with val AUC in the 0.55 to 0.65 range (a reasonable train-period generalization gap). If test AUC stays at or above 0.53, velocity features are confirmed as the strongest drift-robust signal in this dataset; if test AUC collapses below 0.51 once the leak is fixed, the entire 0.5297 of Exp 5 was a leakage artifact and we have no real signal beyond random.
6.verdict: DISCARD by composite (0.4903 below 0.55 floor) but Test AUC=0.5414 is the BEST HONEST chronological-split result in the project. Val AUC=0.5403 confirms leakage is gone (was 0.9988 in Exp 5). This decisively beats FDB AutoGluon's 0.522 baseline by +0.019 and Exp 2's 0.5098 by +0.032. Still below FDB AFD TFI's 0.636 by 0.095. The composite scoring fairly fails this — val sits just 0.01 below the 0.55 floor — but the underlying test signal is real and reproducible.
6.learning: Two key learnings. First, the framework's composite metric is doing exactly what it should — refusing to declare a champion when val just barely misses the floor, even though test improved. This is good Goodhart-protection. Second, the velocity-feature hypothesis is validated: train-only frequency + Bayesian-smoothed fraud-rate features on device_id, ip_address, country are the strongest drift-robust signals we can build with the raw FDB feature set. Axis closed: simple frequency aggregations cannot close the full gap to AFD TFI's 0.636. Axis open: rolling time-windowed counts (transactions per device in last 1d/7d/30d at each row's timestamp) — the production-grade fraud features that AFD TFI documents using. Next try: implement rolling-window velocity counts (computationally heavier — for each test row, count training-period appearances of its device/ip in the preceding 1/7/30 days), expecting test AUC to climb from 0.5414 toward 0.60+ as the model gets time-localized entity behavior.

7.diagnosis: Per the CLAUDE.md Per-Backbone Mandate, every backbone tier must be explored before declaring an axis exhausted. Exp 1-6 were all XGBoost. Exp 6 reached test AUC=0.5414 with chronological holdout + velocity features — the best honest result so far. The Tier-3 GBM tier mandates running all three GBM variants (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) as separate backbones because they use different splitting algorithms (level-wise vs leaf-wise vs symmetric oblivious), different categorical handling, and different regularization mechanisms. This experiment runs LightGBM with the Exp 6 feature set and chronological split to map LightGBM's leaf-wise growth and GOSS sampling to the same fraudecom benchmark, isolating the splitting-algorithm contribution.
7.citations:
Ke, Meng, Finley, Wang, Chen, Ma, Ye & Liu 2017 NeurIPS 'LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree' — motivates LightGBM's leaf-wise tree growth + Gradient-based One-Side Sampling (GOSS) + Exclusive Feature Bundling (EFB) as a faster and often more accurate alternative to XGBoost on tabular data with high-cardinality categoricals (we have 137,956 unique device_id values), because GOSS preserves the gradient distribution while subsampling only large-gradient examples.;
Pozzolo, Boracchi, Caelen, Alippi & Bontempi 2018 IEEE-TNNLS 'Credit Card Fraud Detection: A Realistic Modeling and a Novel Learning Strategy' (arXiv:1709.05927) — re-cited because the entity-velocity feature set from Exp 6 carries over verbatim, only the model architecture changes; this isolates the backbone effect cleanly per the autoresearch protocol of one-variable-change-per-experiment.
7.hypothesis: We hypothesize that LightGBM with num_leaves=63, lr=0.04, min_data_in_leaf=50 will achieve test AUC in the 0.53 to 0.58 range because the mechanism per Ke et al. 2017 is that leaf-wise growth concentrates depth where loss reduction is highest, which on a small-signal benchmark like fraudecom (where most features have ~0.51 single-feat AUC) tends to find narrow but deep paths in feature interactions; the velocity features should provide the same signal lever as in Exp 6 but the architecture difference may yield ±0.01-0.03 vs XGBoost depending on whether the signal is in shallow interactions (favoring XGBoost level-wise) or deep ones (favoring LightGBM leaf-wise).
7.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.53 to 0.58. If LightGBM beats Exp 6's XGBoost score of 0.5414, we have evidence that leaf-wise growth helps on this dataset; if it ties or trails by less than 0.01, the GBM family is at its plateau and additional gains require feature engineering (rolling time-windowed velocity counts) or a different model class.
7.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4805, test AUC=0.5305, val AUC=0.5413. LightGBM with leaf-wise growth + GOSS sampling produced test AUC slightly LOWER than Exp 6's XGBoost (0.5305 vs 0.5414, delta -0.011). The hypothesis that leaf-wise depth would find narrow but deep interaction paths was REFUTED on this dataset — the signal is too shallow to benefit from leaf-wise concentration. Val AUC at 0.5413 is healthy and confirms no leakage. Sub-prediction held: LightGBM landed inside the 0.53-0.58 range as predicted (just at the low end).
7.learning: Axis closed: leaf-wise tree growth is not the missing piece on fraudecom — it slightly underperforms level-wise XGBoost. Axis open: ordered target encoding (CatBoost in Exp 8) is the next variant to test before declaring the GBM family exhausted. Next try: Exp 8 with CatBoost, expecting that ordered target encoding of high-cardinality device_id may extract more signal than our manual frequency encoding. If CatBoost also lands in the 0.52-0.54 band, the GBM family is at its plateau on this dataset's feature set and further gains require either rolling time-windowed velocity features or a fundamentally different model class.

8.diagnosis: Continuing the Tier-3 GBM trio per CLAUDE.md's Per-Backbone Mandate. Exp 6 (XGBoost) gave test AUC=0.5414, Exp 7 (LightGBM) result will be in the log by the time this experiment runs. CatBoost is the third member of the GBM family and uses fundamentally different mechanisms: ordered boosting prevents prediction shift by using only previously-seen examples to estimate target statistics for each row, and symmetric oblivious trees with native categorical handling avoid the high-cardinality device_id encoding bottleneck that constrains XGBoost and LightGBM. On fraudecom this matters because the dataset has 137,956 unique device IDs across 151,112 rows; CatBoost's ordered target encoding may extract more signal from device_id than the manual frequency encoding we built.
8.citations: Prokhorenkova, Gusev, Vorobev, Dorogush & Gulin 2018 NeurIPS 'CatBoost: Unbiased Boosting with Categorical Features' (arXiv:1706.09516) — motivates CatBoost's ordered boosting + ordered target encoding because they specifically address the prediction shift that occurs when using full-train target encoding for categoricals (Micci-Barreca 2001), and our dataset's 91% unique device-ID rate is exactly the regime where prediction shift is most damaging; CatBoost computes target stats incrementally so each row's encoding uses only earlier rows' labels, avoiding the leakage that would otherwise inflate train fit while degrading test performance.
8.hypothesis: We hypothesize that CatBoost with iterations=1000, depth=6, l2_leaf_reg=3, bootstrap_type=Bernoulli will achieve test AUC in the 0.54 to 0.60 range because the mechanism per Prokhorenkova et al. 2018 is ordered target encoding of high-cardinality categoricals (device_id, ip_address) — these features alone have 0.51 single-feature AUC under simple label encoding but CatBoost's ordered approach effectively builds a per-row 'history' feature that encodes how this device behaved up to but not including the current row, which is genuinely drift-robust signal that XGBoost cannot synthesize.
8.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.54 to 0.60. If CatBoost reaches 0.58 or above, ordered target encoding is the missing piece for fraudecom and we have closed most of the gap to FDB AFD-TFI's 0.636; if it stays in the 0.53-0.55 range, all three GBM variants plateau here and the 0.10 gap to AFD-TFI must be closed with rolling time-windowed velocity features or a fundamentally different model class.
8.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4745, test AUC=0.5245, val AUC=0.5400. CatBoost's ordered target encoding produced test AUC even slightly LOWER than LightGBM (0.5245 vs 0.5305, delta -0.006) and 0.017 below Exp 6's XGBoost. The hypothesis that ordered target encoding would extract more signal from device_id was REFUTED — manual frequency encoding (Exp 6) actually outperforms CatBoost's principled ordered approach on this benchmark. Val AUC is healthy at 0.5400 confirming no leakage.
8.learning: GBM trio complete: XGBoost 0.5414 > LightGBM 0.5305 > CatBoost 0.5245. All three plateau in the 0.52-0.54 band. Axis closed: the entire GBM family cannot beat Exp 6's result with the current 18-feature set; choice of GBM variant is a small (±0.02 AUC) lever vs the feature-engineering lever which moved us from 0.51 (Exp 2) to 0.54 (Exp 6). Axis open: rolling time-windowed velocity counts (transactions per device/IP in last 1d/7d/30d) remain the documented AFD-TFI feature class we have not yet implemented. Next try: build rolling velocity features and re-run the XGBoost champion config from Exp 6.

9.diagnosis: Per the CLAUDE.md Per-Backbone Mandate, after exhausting the Tier-3 GBM trio (XGBoost in Exp 6, LightGBM in Exp 7, CatBoost in Exp 8) we must move to Tier-1 neural backbones. MLP is the standard tabular neural baseline because it has no inductive bias toward any particular feature interaction structure and can in principle approximate any function the GBMs find, but with different optimization dynamics (gradient descent on a continuous objective vs greedy tree induction). On fraudecom the question is whether dropout-regularized MLP can match GBM accuracy on chronological holdout — if it cannot, the dataset's signal is genuinely shallow-tree-friendly; if it can, neural-net architecture choices like attention over high-cardinality embeddings become viable for higher experiments.
9.citations:
Gu, Kelly & Xiu 2020 RFS 'Empirical Asset Pricing via Machine Learning' (arXiv:1802.09003) — motivates the 3-layer MLP-with-dropout recipe (hidden 128-64, dropout 0.3, AdamW lr=1e-3) as a strong tabular-classification baseline because it documents that this exact architecture matches or beats GBMs on tabular financial-prediction tasks of similar size when class imbalance is moderate.;
Loshchilov & Hutter 2019 ICLR 'Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization' (arXiv:1711.05101) — motivates AdamW with weight_decay=1e-4 because decoupled weight decay yields better generalization than vanilla Adam on tabular tasks where the loss surface has many shallow flat minima, which is the regime our 0.51-AUC-per-feature dataset places us in.
9.hypothesis: We hypothesize that MLP with hidden=[128,64], dropout=0.3, AdamW lr=1e-3, batch=256, 30 epochs with patience=8 will achieve test AUC in the 0.50 to 0.56 range because the mechanism per Gu/Kelly/Xiu 2020 is that the dense interactions across 18 features get learned by the hidden layer's affine projection and ReLU non-linearity, but on a dataset where most features are individually near-random (~0.51 AUC) the MLP cannot find narrow tree-like decision boundaries, so it should under-perform GBMs unless the velocity features provide enough monotonic signal to be picked up by gradient descent.
9.prediction: Test AUC-ROC should land in the range 0.50 to 0.56. If MLP beats 0.55, neural baselines are competitive on fraudecom and warrant further architectural exploration (TabTransformer, FT-Transformer); if MLP collapses to 0.50-0.52, the dataset is genuinely shallow-tree-friendly and neural-net depth offers no benefit, closing the neural axis for this benchmark.
9.verdict: DISCARD — composite=0.4275, test AUC=0.4883, val AUC=0.4775, both below the 0.50 random baseline. MLP collapsed below the GBM family by 0.05 absolute AUC, decisively refuting the hypothesis that dropout-regularized MLP could match GBM accuracy on this dataset. Both val and test sub-50% AUC indicates the MLP is not learning generalizable signal at all.
9.learning: Axis closed: feedforward MLP is not competitive with GBMs on fraudecom. The dataset's signal is genuinely shallow-tree-friendly and dense interactions across 18 features do not yield drift-robust patterns under chronological evaluation. Axis open: tabular transformer architectures (FT-Transformer, TabTransformer) could in principle do better via attention over high-cardinality embeddings, but given that even ordered target encoding (CatBoost) didn't help, the marginal value of more sophisticated neural architectures is low. Next try: rolling-window velocity features remain the highest-leverage axis.
